routes.description: Establish a historically supported set of facts concerning Jesus's death and its aftermath, defend their reliability, and show that divine resurrection explains them better than the relevant skeptical alternatives within an independently supported theistic context.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if the relevant historical facts are sufficiently established and the resurrection hypothesis compares favorably with naturalistic rivals in explanatory power, scope, plausibility, and fit with the available evidence.

motionBridge.description: Connect the established historical facts and comparative explanatory analysis to the conclusion that Jesus's resurrection is their best historical explanation.

centralBridges.description: Establish the crucifixion, burial, empty tomb, postmortem experiences, and transformation of the disciples as historical facts requiring explanation.
Ground the appearance and empty-tomb traditions in sufficiently early, multiple, and independent historical sources rather than late legendary development.
Show that conspiracy, hallucination, mistake, and legendary-development accounts lack the explanatory power, scope, or historical plausibility needed to explain the relevant facts.
Supply a theistic context in which divine action is antecedently possible enough for resurrection to compete seriously in the explanatory comparison.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Defend probabilistic inference to the best explanation as an appropriate form of historical proof without requiring mathematical certainty.
Explain how ordinary historical evidence can support an extraordinary event when the evidence is substantially more expected if that event occurred.

routes.description: Prevent the resurrection conclusion by challenging the reliability and sufficiency of the alleged historical facts, contesting the standards used to infer a supernatural event, and preserving naturalistic or agnostic alternatives as comparatively credible.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if evidential uncertainty, source-development concerns, unfavorable prior probability, or viable skeptical alternatives make the resurrection inference insufficiently established as the best explanation of the facts.

motionBridge.description: Connect unresolved historical and comparative uncertainties to the conclusion that the evidence does not warrant treating resurrection as the best explanation.

centralBridges.description: Distinguish historical support for surrounding reports and events from direct establishment of the supernatural resurrection asserted to explain them.
Show that sparse, uneven, or progressively elaborated appearance traditions weaken confidence in the facts entered into the explanatory comparison.
Preserve sincere mistake, grief-related experience, legendary development, or other naturalistic possibilities without requiring deliberate disciple deception.
Account for the antecedent improbability of divine resurrection when comparing it with naturalistic explanations, especially absent an accepted theistic framework.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Justify heightened evidential caution for a uniquely extraordinary and morally consequential supernatural claim.
Test whether the quantity and clarity of the historical record fit the hypothesis that an omnipotent God strongly intends widespread belief in the resurrection.

sections.title: Historical Proof and the Evidential Standard
sections.rationale: This issue determines what historical inquiry must establish, whether inference to the best explanation counts as proof, and whether the extraordinary character and significance of resurrection alter the evidential threshold.

sections.title: Prior Probability and Theistic Context
sections.rationale: The comparative plausibility of resurrection depends materially on whether divine action is assessed within an independently supported theistic context or from a framework assigning miracles an exceptionally unfavorable prior probability.

sections.title: Core Historical Facts and Source Reliability
sections.rationale: The explanatory contest depends on which facts are sufficiently established, including the empty tomb and postmortem experiences, and on whether early, multiple, and independent sources reliably support them.

sections.title: Naturalistic Alternatives and Explanatory Fit
sections.rationale: The motion requires comparison between resurrection and skeptical alternatives, including conspiracy, sincere mistake, hallucination, and legendary development, across explanatory scope, power, and historical plausibility.

sections.title: Divine Purpose, Evidential Clarity, and Practical Stakes
sections.rationale: This issue tests whether the available evidence fits an asserted divine desire for belief and clarifies whether practical consequences bear on warranted belief separately from the historical case itself.
